wily

/WY-lee/ - rhymes with highly · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Wily means clever at getting what one wants through trickery.

The wily quartermaster requisitioned double what he needed, knowing headquarters took pride in cutting every request in half.

Worked Example

Grandmother was the wiliest seller at the fair: she entered the pie contest with her second-best recipe, let a neighbor take the ribbon, and sold out her stall by noon while the winner was still giving interviews.

Wily is trickery in the service of getting what you want, and it usually carries a grin. A resourceful person improvises honestly, and an underhanded one has crossed into plain dishonesty — the wily one works the angles: misdirection, side doors, letting you win the wrong prize.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tricky: Tricky is the everyday word for wily, with less admiration in it — a tricky opponent uses deception, and the word is a warning. Wily carries a grin: it praises the skill in the trickery, the fox working the angles, even while it admits the tricks are tricks.

slippery: Slippery describes someone hard to pin down or hold to any promise — ask a direct question and the answer squirms away. Wily is more active: the wily work angles and set traps to get what they want, while the slippery mainly escape. A wily fox hunts; a slippery one avoids being caught.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

artless: has no tricks in the toolbox at all

honest: gets what it wants by asking straight out

Where it sits · how far outside the rules it operates — resourceful → wily → underhanded

resourceful vs. wily: Resourceful is milder than wily — the resourceful improvise their way to a goal without fooling anyone.

underhanded vs. wily: Underhanded goes further than wily: wily bends the rules with a wink and a trick, while underhanded breaks them outright in the dark.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — wil-

Root — wil-: a sly trick (from wile)

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Wily is wile plus -y: 'full of wiles.' A wile is a single sly trick — and the word may descend from the same Norman stock as guile, this unit's own name for the talent, making wily and guile long-lost cousins. English still says someone 'used all her wiles'; wily is what you call the person who keeps a full set.

Use the root on its own: wile

Use the root on its own: wile: The peddler's oldest wile was pretending to pack up early, which reliably doubled the crowd at his cart.

Word Choice

informal / admiring

Wily sits at the likable end of this unit's trickster row: it praises skillful, usually low-stakes trickery — foxes, grandmothers, veterans of long queues. Cunning is its cooler twin and can turn sinister; guile names the raw talent. Where no trickery is involved at all, the honest compliment is resourceful.
